blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Texture Networks paper as a breakthrough that enables fast, memory-efficient texture synthesis and image stylization, which powers apps like Prisma. The paper contrasts with Gatys et al.'s earlier approach, which required 10 seconds and 1.1GB of memory per image, while Ulyanov et al.'s method achieves similar quality in just 20ms and 170MB. The key insight is replacing Gatys' iterative optimization with a feed-forward neural network trained per texture/style, enabling real-time generation. Colyer notes the potential for applying this to video processing and praises the broader applicability of feed-forward networks for complex data generation tasks.
paper_title: Texture Networks: Feed-forward synthesis of textures and stylized images
paper_abstract: Gatys et al. recently demonstrated that deep networks can generate beautiful textures and stylized images from a single texture example. However, their methods requires a slow and memoryconsuming optimization process. We propose here an alternative approach that moves the computational burden to a learning stage. Given a single example of a texture, our approach trains compact feed-forward convolutional networks to generate multiple samples of the same texture of arbitrary size and to transfer artistic style from a given image to any other image. The resulting networks are remarkably light-weight and can generate textures of quality comparable to Gatys et al., but hundreds of times faster. More generally, our approach highlights the power and flexibility of generative feed-forward models trained with complex and expressive loss functions.

figures.title: Comparison of texture synthesis methods
figures.caption: Texture networks proposed in this work are feed-forward architectures capable of learning to synthesize complex textures based on a single training example. The perceptual quality of the feed-forwardly generated textures is similar to the results of the closely related method suggested in (Gatys et al., 2015a), which use slow optimization process.
